title: Analysis: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use - Carbon Brief
gist: The Global Carbon Project's 2026 carbon budget projects fossil CO2 falling ~0.4% to 38.2GtCO2 (range -1.5% to +0.6%), driven by a 1.9% oil drop after the Iran conflict closed the strait of Hormuz, while El Niño-linked land-use emissions push total CO2 to a record 43.3GtCO2. A companion Nature Climate Change study finds solar, wind and EVs offset ~69% of demand-driven emissions growth, so the dip is a price shock, not a peak.

insights.claim: The Global Carbon Project projects fossil-fuel and cement CO2 emissions to fall about 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2GtCO2, with an uncertainty range from -1.5% to +0.6%, so a small increase cannot be ruled out.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A rare fossil-emissions decline is fragile; do not price in a structural peak yet.
insights.locator: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels

insights.claim: Total CO2 emissions including land use are projected at a record 43.3GtCO2 in 2026, up from 42.8GtCO2 in 2025, with the increase coming entirely from higher land-use emissions; had land use stayed flat, totals would have fallen to about 42.6GtCO2.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Headline 'record emissions' stories will coexist with falling fossil emissions; land-use volatility matters for offset/nature markets.
insights.locator: Total emissions edge up as land-use emissions rise

insights.claim: Total CO2 emissions grew 0.3% per year over 2016-25 versus 1.7% per year over 2006-15, and fossil emissions grew about 0.9% per year versus 1.9%, a plateau but far from the rapid declines needed for net zero.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Emissions growth has structurally slowed, consistent with saturating fossil demand growth in major economies.
insights.locator: The updated numbers show that total emissions

insights.claim: This year's Global Carbon Budget revises historical fossil emissions up by about 0.3GtCO2 per year because it now assumes a smaller cement carbonation sink, i.e. cement reabsorbs less CO2 over its lifetime than previously thought.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Cement decarbonization becomes marginally more important; less credit for passive carbonation.
insights.locator: This year's estimates of historical fossil emissions

insights.claim: Global per-capita fossil emissions peaked in the early 2010s and are around 4.6 tonnes per person in 2026, about 4% below peak; India's 2025 per-capita emissions are 2.2 tonnes versus 14.5 tonnes in the US.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: India's low per-capita base implies long runway for energy (and coal) demand growth.
insights.locator: Global per-capita fossil emissions peaked

insights.claim: Global oil emissions are projected to fall 1.9% in 2026 (243MtCO2), one of the largest annual falls on record outside 2020's Covid collapse, comparable to 2009 and 1992, driven by higher prices and reduced output after the Iran conflict closed the strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Demand destruction from the Hormuz shock is material; watch whether oil demand rebounds once supply normalizes.
insights.locator: Oil is the main driver of the decline

insights.claim: Petrol and diesel prices in the US, China and the EU were 10-50% higher in 2026 than in 2025, depending on the fuel and period.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Quantifies the retail fuel-price shock behind 2026 oil demand weakness.
insights.locator: Petrol and diesel prices in the US

insights.claim: EV growth accounted for around a fifth of the overall drop in global oil emissions in 2026, with the rest mostly attributed to high prices and supply constraints.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: EV substitution is now a visible, non-trivial driver of oil demand loss even within a price shock.
insights.locator: A study published in parallel by the team

insights.claim: Oil emissions are projected to fall in every major region in 2026, with the largest drop in China at -4.6%; international aviation and shipping are each projected to fall 1%, partly from reduced Middle East traffic.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: China's oil demand weakness is a key bearish signal for crude; shipping/aviation volumes hit by Middle East disruption.

insights.claim: Global oil emissions in 2026 remain only about 1% above their 2019 pre-pandemic level.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Oil demand has effectively plateaued since 2019, supporting peak-oil-demand theses.
insights.locator: Oil emissions remain about 1% above

insights.claim: China's fossil emissions (32% of global) are projected to fall 0.9% in 2026 after two years of low growth, with oil -4.6%, gas -0.9% and coal +0.3%, attributed to strong renewables growth and milder summer temperatures; it remains too early to call a peak.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: China's coal flatlining plus oil decline is negative for seaborne coal/crude demand growth.
insights.locator: China32%

insights.claim: US fossil emissions are projected to fall 1.3% in 2026, mainly from a 6.7% drop in coal emissions after an unusual 2025 rise driven by high gas prices and cold weather; US gas emissions rose 0.5%.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: US coal burn is gas-price sensitive; 2025's coal rebound was transitory.
insights.locator: US13%

insights.claim: India's fossil emissions are projected to rise 4.4% in 2026, above its 3.5% decade average, with coal up 5.9% while oil falls 0.9%.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: India is the main growth market for coal; supportive for coal suppliers to India.
insights.locator: India8%

insights.claim: EU fossil emissions are projected to fall 1.5% in 2026 (coal -2.9%, oil -1.8%), and Japan's by 1.0% as transport electrifies, population ages and nuclear plants restart.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Japan's nuclear restarts structurally reduce fossil import demand.
insights.locator: EU6%

insights.claim: Global coal emissions are projected to rise 0.6% in 2026 while gas is effectively flat (-0.3%); coal accounts for about 41% of fossil CO2, oil 33%, gas 21% and cement 2%.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Coal remains the largest single emissions source and the main area where growth persists (India).
insights.locator: Coal accounts for around 41%

insights.claim: Coal emissions grew around 4% per year in the 2000s but only slightly since 2013, leaving 2026 coal emissions just about 6% above 2013 levels.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Global coal is in a long plateau rather than growth phase.
insights.locator: Coal emissions grew rapidly in the 2000s

insights.claim: Forty countries accounting for 26% of global fossil emissions significantly cut emissions while growing their economies over 2016-25, up from 22 countries in the previous decade.

insights.so_what: Decoupling of GDP and emissions is spreading, undermining the growth-vs-climate trade-off argument.

insights.claim: Land-use emissions are projected to rise to 5.1GtCO2 in 2026 from 4.4GtCO2 in 2025, driven by mostly human-ignited peat fires and forest degradation in south-east Asia during drier El Niño conditions.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: El Niño years raise land-use emissions and weaken sinks; relevant to nature-based carbon credit risk.
insights.locator: Land-use emissions are projected to rise to 5.1GtCO2

insights.claim: Net land-use emissions averaged 4.9GtCO2 per year over 2016-25, about 21% below the 6.2GtCO2 of 2006-15, a decline consistent across all three bookkeeping models.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Deforestation trends have improved on a decadal basis.
insights.locator: Net land-use emissions averaged 4.9GtCO2

insights.claim: Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Indonesia together accounted for 2.6GtCO2 per year of land-use emissions over 2015-25, around 54% of the global total.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff

insights.claim: The land carbon sink hit a record of about 13.3GtCO2 in 2025, 50% larger than 2024, rebounding in the tropics after the 2023-24 El Niño; the El Niño that began in June 2026 is expected to weaken the sink mainly in 2027.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Expect a faster atmospheric CO2 rise in 2027 as the sink weakens.

insights.claim: Atmospheric CO2 is projected to rise 2.2ppm in 2026 to an average 427.7ppm, about 54% above pre-industrial, versus a record 3.8ppm rise in 2024 during the last El Niño.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Concentration trajectory continues upward regardless of emissions plateau.

insights.claim: With human-caused warming at 1.37C in 2025, the remaining carbon budget for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5C is 150GtCO2 from the start of 2027, less than four years of 2026 emissions; the 1.7C and 2C budgets are 510GtCO2 and 1,035GtCO2 (about 12 and 24 years).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: 1.5C is effectively exhausted; policy and investment frameworks will pivot to 1.7C/2C and overshoot/removal.

insights.claim: A Nature Climate Change study estimates rising energy demand would have added about 0.78GtCO2 in 2026, of which solar, wind and EV growth offset 0.54GtCO2 or about 69%; the remainder of the 2026 decline came from high prices and supply constraints after the Iran conflict.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Clean tech alone is not yet bending the curve; the 2026 decline depends on the oil price shock.

insights.so_what: Fade narratives that 2026 marks peak global emissions; expect rebound if oil prices normalize.
